items.fact: That's a walrus baculum — a penis bone. Walruses have one of the largest of any living mammal, up to around 60 cm. Polished ones are sold in Alaska as 'oosiks'.

sources.title: Baculum
sources.supported_claim: Walrus baculum is among the largest of living mammals; called oosik in Alaska.
sources.review_note: Drafted from general knowledge; needs human fact-check before approval.

items.reveal_line: A walrus. That's a bone. Inside it. Permanently. And people buy them as souvenirs.

items.fact: Snakes have two penises, called hemipenes, tucked into the base of the tail. They use one at a time, and many species' are covered in spines and hooks. This one belongs to the Alcatrazes lancehead, a pit viper found on a single Brazilian island.

sources.title: Hemipenis
sources.supported_claim: Snakes and lizards have paired hemipenes, used one at a time, often spiny.
sources.review_note: Drafted from general knowledge; needs human fact-check before approval.

items.fact: Male spiders have no penis at all. They spin a tiny web, deposit sperm on it, soak it up into bulbs on their pedipalps — the little arms by the mouth — and deliver it with those. This is the palp of a grey house spider.

sources.title: Spider — reproduction
sources.supported_claim: Males transfer sperm with their pedipalps after charging them from a sperm web.
sources.review_note: Drafted from general knowledge; needs human fact-check before approval.

items.fact: Male octopuses mate with a specially modified arm called the hectocotylus. In some relatives the arm breaks off inside the female. When Georges Cuvier first found one, he thought it was a parasitic worm and gave it its name.

sources.title: Hectocotylus
sources.supported_claim: Modified arm used to transfer sperm; may detach in argonauts; Cuvier first described it as a parasite.
sources.review_note: Drafted from general knowledge; needs human fact-check before approval.

items.fact: Many land snails stab their partner with a 'love dart' made of calcium before mating. The mucus on the dart improves the chances the stabber's sperm is used. This is the dart of the Asian tramp snail, under an electron microscope.

sources.title: Love dart
sources.supported_claim: Calcareous dart used in snail courtship; mucus improves sperm survival.

items.fact: Beetle penises, called aedeagi, differ so much between species that entomologists often use them to tell species apart. This one belongs to a marsh beetle, Cyphon poecilopterus.

items.fact: Male guppies and their relatives have a gonopodium: a fin that has evolved into a mating organ and swings forward to deliver sperm. This is from Endler's livebearer, a close cousin of the guppy.

items.fact: It isn't a genital at all. It's a fungus: the common stinkhorn. Its scientific name, Phallus impudicus, means 'shameless penis', and its slimy tip smells of rotting meat to attract flies.

sources.title: Phallus impudicus
sources.supported_claim: Common stinkhorn; name means shameless penis; foul smell attracts flies.

items.fact: It isn't a genital either. It's the neck — properly, the siphon — of a geoduck, a giant clam from the Pacific Northwest. Geoducks can live for well over a century.

sources.title: Pacific geoduck
sources.supported_claim: Large burrowing clam with a long siphon; can live over 150 years.
